Female Coates (Carcharhinus coatesi) attain a maximum asymptotic body length of 88 cm [Li = 88 cm], a value derived from field surveys of mature individuals across northern Australian waters. In contrast, males reach a slightly smaller ultimate total length of 87 cm [Li = 87 cm], indicating a modest degree of sexual dimorphism in this small-bodied requiem shark. Examination of growth curves from vertebral ring counts suggests that females continue to expand somatic size for a longer portion of their lifespan relative to males, a pattern observed in many carcharhinid sharks. The relationship between length and mass follows a power curve estimated from a large sample of dissected specimens; applying the equation 0.00479 times length raised to the 3.10 power yields an asymptotic wet body mass for adult females of approximately 5.1 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 5.1 kilograms]. This mass is relatively low compared to most members of the genus Carcharhinus, consistent with the species' small maximum stature. Pregnant females carrying term embryos are frequently encountered in trawl surveys, allowing robust estimation of these length-based parameters across multiple geographic populations.

Neonatal Coates are born at a total length of approximately 39 cm [Lb = approximately 39 cm], with reported values typically ranging from 38 to 40 cm, based on the examination of near-term embryos removed from gravid females captured in coastal gill-net surveys. This size at birth is modest relative to congeneric species such as Carcharhinus limbatus, but appears well-suited to the shallow, turbid nursery habitats the pups occupy along the tropical continental shelf. Following parturition, the yolk-sac stage is brief, and neonates rapidly undergo the trophic switch to independent foraging on small teleosts and crustaceans. Growth during the first year is comparatively rapid, with vertebral growth bands indicating that animals approximately double their birth length by the end of their initial 12 months. The age at birth for free-living pups captured immediately postpartum has been inferred from the timing of the breeding season, with parturition occurring after a gestation period of approximately 292 days [ab = approximately 292 days] when ambient water temperatures hover near 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This gestation length aligns well with values reported for other small-bodied carcharhinids with similar reproductive modes.

Sexual maturation in female Coates is attained at a total length of roughly 70 cm [Lp = roughly 70 cm], a body size corresponding to approximately 80% of their ultimate asymptotic size. This threshold was established through histological examination of ovarian tissue in specimens collected across multiple seasons; the presence of enlarged vitellogenic follicles and corpora lutea was used to confirm reproductive status. Males achieve comparable gonadal development at slightly smaller sizes, a typical pattern in elasmobranchs wherein testicular recrudescence precedes full female maturity. The size at puberty appears relatively invariant across the species' range, suggesting a strong genetic or physiological constraint rather than a purely environmental influence. Females bearing developing ova and recently formed egg capsules are seldom captured below this length, supporting the robustness of the observation that females reach the pubertal length of 70 cm before initiating reproduction. This finding is consistent with life-history theory predicting delayed maturation in species that produce small numbers of well-developed offspring, as the energetic demands of gestation are considerable.

Under thermal conditions characteristic of its tropical habitat, with water temperatures consistently near 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the maximum reproductive output of Coates is modest. Females produce litters containing from 1 to 3 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 3 pups per litter], and available data from long-term capture-mark-recapture studies suggest that individual females breed approximately once every two years [F_R_i = approximately once every two years]. This biennial reproductive cycle is common among small carcharhinid sharks and likely reflects the energetic cost of supporting a lengthy gestation followed by a period of post-partum recovery and yolk production. The combination of small litter size and low reproductive frequency means that population-level recruitment is relatively slow, making the species potentially vulnerable to localized overfishing. The 26 °C isotherm broadly defines the core of the species' distribution, and deviations from this thermal regime may influence inter-birth intervals. Marked females recaptured after multiple seasons provide the most reliable estimates of this slow reproductive schedule.

Maximum longevity in Coates appears to be approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years], a figure based on the oldest back-calculated ages obtained from vertebral growth bands under the assumption that the maximum recorded age closely approximates natural lifespan at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]in this system. All age estimates were derived from individuals sampled in waters maintained at a stable temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], reflecting the species' preference for warm tropical environments. This lifespan is comparatively short for a member of the genus Carcharhinus, many of which regularly exceed 15 years, and likely correlates with the species' small body size and relatively high metabolic rate. The rapid life-history pace means that generation turnover is fairly swift, with most individuals completing their reproductive lives within a 5- to 6-year window of maturity. Future studies employing bomb radiocarbon dating or tag-recapture modeling could refine this estimate, but current vertebral ageing provides a consistent picture of a relatively short-lived elasmobranch. The natural mortality rate inferred from this maximum age aligns with expectations for a teleost-feeding predator of moderate abundance.
